newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lufthansa must excite on Asia - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Lufthansa must excite on Asia - analysts.

text.p: Germany's Lufthansa and its four existing partners must give clues on possible new link-ups, particularly in Asia, if they are to excite with Wednesday's unveiling of a global airline alliance, analysts said on Tuesday.

Aviation experts said that while the focus of the rival British Airways -AMR link-up was clearly the north Atlantic routes, the Lufthansa grouping could yet steal a march in the expanding markets of the east.

"Lufthansa is already talking to one, maybe two potential Asian partners. If it were to mention specific names, the announcement will be seen positively," Juergen Trojan, an analyst at Frankfurt-based Independent Research said.

With code-sharing deals already in place with Thai International Airways, the partnership of Lufthansa, United Airlines, Air Canada and Scandinavian Airline System already has a foothold in the region.

But analysts highlighted Asia as the current weak link in the grouping and cited the strongly-rumoured Cathay Pacific of Hong Kong as one airline that would significantly bolster its operations there.
Lufthansa itself has declined to comment on specific talks but chairman Juergen Weber said in March that agreements for the region should be struck by the end of the year.
Outside Asia, attention will focus on Lufthansa's growing relationship with British Midland, with whom it signed code-sharing agreements last month covering London Heathrow, Cologne and Rome.

"With British Midland, however, I believe it will be more a case of developing existing cooperation rather than taking it on as a fixed partner," Juergen Pieper, analyst for Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said.

Pieper said he expected Wednesday's announcement to concentrate on the possibilities thrown up by the creation of a single brandname for the alliance, which among other things could lead to joint advertising and marketing programmes.
"This kind of loose alliance not involving share transactions can produce a number of advantages with very few risks," Pieper said.
The five airlines are widely believed to have chosen the name "Star Alliance" for the link-up, a tag that none of them has officially confirmed.

Little in the way of regulatory problems are expected to be encountered as the alliance gradually develops, precisely because it would be perceived as offering a welcome global competitor to the BA/AMR grouping.
"My feeling is that regulatory authorities will be inclined to accept it. Above all, its market position on the north Atlantic route is far behind that of BA/AMR," said Trojan.
If indeed the future direction of the alliance were in Asia, the five partners could expect little regulatory intervention there, he added.
